title: A Bent Wire Missed Its Target, Yet Rats Pressed a Lever 7,500 Times
description:
Myth vs. Neural Mechanism — James Olds & Peter Milner (1954): Accidental Septal-Mesolimbic Brain Stimulation & 7,500 Lever Presses, grounded in James Olds, Peter Milner (1954) (Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology). Empirical findings show that in late 1953 at McGill University (published 1954), postdoc James Olds aimed a fine insulated silver wire electrode at a rat's midbrain reticular activating system, where stimulation normally caused avoidance.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how nucleus accumbens, ventral tegmental area, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that during implantation, the flexible wire bent forward by several millimeters, landing in the anterior septal / medial forebrain bundle region instead — verified later by post-mortem X-ray and histology.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- James Olds, Peter Milner (1954). Positive reinforcement produced by electrical stimulation of septal area and other regions of rat brain. Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0058775
- Roy A. Wise (2004). Dopamine, learning and motivation. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn1406
- Kent C. Berridge, Morten L. Kringelbach (2015). Pleasure Systems in the Brain. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.02.018

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
